item.title: Egyptian editor faces trial after hours of questioning
item.description:
Egyptian editor faces trial after hours of questioning
Egyptian prosecutors referred Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of independent news outlet Mada Masr, to trial on a charge of operating a website without a license, after questioning her for more than six hoursByThe Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 4:18 PM
Share
The editor-in-chief of one of Egypt’s last independent news outlets, Mada Masr, will stand trial after prosecutors questioned her for more than six hours, her lawyer said early Thursday.
The Supreme State Prosecution referred Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah to trial on Thursday on a charge of establishing and managing a website without a license. She was also questioned on a charge of publishing false news, but that charge was not included in her court referral, according to Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari.
She was released Wednesday evening on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds ($1,800), but if convicted, she faces a fine of one to three million Egyptian pounds ($18,000 to $54,000), al-Azhari said.
Under Egyptian media law, the court may also order the outlet closed and its equipment confiscated. Al-Azhari called the speed of the referral, which came just hours after the questioning ended, “unjustified urgency.”
Attalah is due in court on Oct. 27.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, and its investigative reporting has made it a frequent target of authorities. The site has been blocked in Egypt since 2017. Time magazine named Attalah one of its 100 most influential people in 2020.
The case file included a Mada Masr report published earlier this month in which lawyers described a wave of protests at several prisons and a harsh security response, al-Azhari said. The protests followed parliament’s decision to delay Egypt’s new criminal procedures law by a year.

item.title: Twice a year, a golden sunbeam illuminates a 3,000-year-old Egyptian temple
item.description:
Twice a year, a golden sunbeam illuminates a 3,000-year-old Egyptian temple
Tourists and locals gathered at a temple in southern Egypt on Thursday to witness a rare solar phenomenonTwice a year, a golden sunbeam illuminates a 3,000-year-old Egyptian templeThe Associated PressByHAMZA FAHMY Associated Press and MOHAMMED SALAH Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 12:26 PM
Share
ABU SIMBEL, Egypt -- Hundreds of tourists from around the world and locals gathered at dawn Thursday at a temple in southern Egypt, with some sleeping outside it overnight to witness a solar phenomenon that has taken place here for millennia.
Twice a year, on Oct. 22 and Feb. 22 — dates believed to mark the ascension of Ramesses II to the throne and his birthday — the sun sends a beam of light into the Great Temple of Ramses II’s dark inner chamber to illuminate the statues of the pharaoh and two gods beside him.
The illumination, a result of the temple's alignment with the sun, lasts about 20 minutes.
“Today is a very special day, as you can see. It’s a celebration and a historic holiday," Hisham Khela, a local tour guide for Italian tourists, told The Associated Press.
Egyptology enthusiasts and other visitors stood in a messy single-file line with phone cameras in hand, some with selfie sticks and most with bags under their eyes from waking up so early. Although huge crowds turned up, they looked tiny beside the giant statues lining the temple, which overlooks the Nile.
To mark the phenomenon, colorfully dressed performers scattered in front of the temple smiled and danced in unison to meditative chimes, the percussion of the tabla and the distinct sound of mizmars, an ancient Egyptian trumpet.
Inside the temple, visitors huddled tightly in near-total darkness in front of the statues of Ramesses II and the gods Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty, lit by a beam of sunlight that traveled about 60 meters (200 feet) into the temple, according to the National Research Institute of Astronomy and ...

item.title: A magnitude 7 earthquake shakes China's Tibet
item.description:
A magnitude 7 earthquake shakes China's Tibet
A magnitude 7 earthquake has struck China’s Tibet on Thursday evening, with no immediate reports of damage or casualtiesByThe Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 12:07 PM
BEIJING -- A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China’s Tibet on Thursday evening, with no immediate reports of damage or casualties.
The United States Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles).
China’s official Xinhua News Agency cited the China Earthquake Networks Center as putting the depth at 10 kilometers (6.2 miles).

item.title: Brazil's Congress's shift to the right could change Latin America's powerhouse. Here’s what to know
item.description:
Brazil's Congress's shift to the right could change Latin America's powerhouse. Here’s what to know
Brazil’s elections have shifted Congress further right, regardless of who wins the presidential runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da SilvaByMAURICIO SAVARESE Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 9:34 AM
SAO PAULO -- Brazil’s elections have shifted its Congress to the right regardless of who wins Sunday's presidential runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Many lawmakers taking office in February 2027 are keen to reshape the nation’s Supreme Court, economy, human rights protections and environmental policies.
If right-wing and centrist lawmakers unite, they will command a simple majority in the 513-seat lower house and could even assemble a supermajority in a broad alliance to change Brazil’s constitution. A similar dynamic is expected in the Senate. Analysts and politicians agree there could be long-lasting impacts in Brazil and in Latin America.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won an additional 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubled its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties. Lula's Workers' Party held onto roughly the same number of seats.
Those figures could still change as some lawmakers change parties after their election.
Here is a look at how this right-leaning Congress could reshape Brazil’s agenda.
Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that put former President Jair Bolsonaro in prison for his attempted coup.
They need 54 votes in the Senate, and many of the future members ran precisely on an impeach de Moraes platform. Brazil’s next president will be able to appoint at least three new justices.

item.title: An Austrian and a Swiss woman freed in Niger after a year and half in captivity
item.description:
An Austrian and a Swiss woman freed in Niger after a year and half in captivity
Two women from Austria and Switzerland have been freed in Niger after spending more than a year and half in captivity, officials and local media reported ThursdayByThe Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 7:46 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NIAMEY, Niger -- Two women from Austria and Switzerland have been freed in Niger after spending more than a year and a half in captivity, officials and local media reported Thursday.
The Austrian woman, an aid worker identified as Eva G, was received by the Austrian crisis team on Thursday, Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said in a statement.
She was kidnapped in Niger’s Agadez city in January last year, months before the Swiss citizen was abducted in the same city in April 2025.
Meinl-Reisinger said Austria worked with Switzerland to find “a safe solution” for the women.
“We are all very relieved that Eva G. is free again after more than 21 months. This time was an unimaginable burden for her and her family,” Meinl-Reisinger said.
Swiss media quoted the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs as confirming the release of the Swiss woman.
Swiss newspaper 20 Minuten reported she was on her way home, quoting Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis.

item.title: Foreign citizen killed during march in South Africa as anti-immigrant tensions flare
item.description:
Foreign citizen killed during march in South Africa as anti-immigrant tensions flare
Police say a foreign citizen has been beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South AfricaByGERALD IMRAY Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 7:07 AM
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- A foreign citizen was beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South Africa's east coast city of Durban, police said Thursday, as anti-immigrant tensions continue to flare in Africa's most advanced economy.
Police said the group approached the man, who was standing at the side of a road during a march through the streets of Durban's city center, and assaulted him.
Police did not immediately give the man's nationality or details on what the march was related to. They said the victim was in his 30s or early 40s, and they were still trying to identify suspects in the attack.
South Africa has struggled with months of anti-immigration tensions. Marches calling for government action against migrants in the country illegally have sometimes spilled over into violence.
Nigeria, Mozambique, Malawi and other countries have said some of their citizens have been killed in xenophobic attacks linked to the anti-immigration protests. South African authorities have disputed some of those claims and said some deaths were related to criminal activity and not the protests.
Tens of thousands of migrants have left South Africa in recent months in one of the biggest mass exoduses in years. Many cite the threat of violence from angry locals, though the government also said that many were deported for not having the proper documents to be in South Africa.
As Africa's biggest economy, South Africa attracts migrants from many nations on the continent, but that has sometimes brought tensions within communities because of the country's extremely high unemployment rate and overburdened public services.

item.title: Serb voters abroad face long trips in tight election after officials move polling stations
item.description:
Serb voters abroad face long trips in tight election after officials move polling stations
Serbian voters overseas are facing major hurdles in casting their ballots in a tight parliamentary election this weekendByBRANIMIR PIPAL Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 6:47 AM
BELGRADE, Serbia -- When Irina Djordjic registered in Canada to vote in an election this weekend in her native Serbia, she expected a repeat of the 2023 poll: a short drive to the consulate in Vancouver for a relaxed Sunday afternoon voting with fellow Serbs. She was wrong.
Djordjic, who holds dual Canadian-Serbian citizenship, was told that her polling station had moved to Toronto, 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) away, and would open at 2 a.m. to match polls opening in the Serbian time zone, where it's 8 a.m.
The decision by the Serbian election authorities meant that she and hundreds of other Serbs in Vancouver would have to take a 4.5-hour flight and possibly line up in the middle of the night to vote. Thousands of Serb expatriates in the United States, Australia and New Zealand face the same problem. Some 100,000 people have registered to vote abroad this year, up from 39,000 in 2023.
Critics say it's a deliberate move to discourage voters abroad, who may be less supportive of populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic as he faces his biggest electoral challenge yet from a youth movement behind almost two years of protests against Vucic's tight rule in the Balkan country. Turnout in Serbia is expected to be high, which is believed to favor the students.
"Some people have small children, some can’t be absent for too long,” Djordjic, a former journalist from Belgrade who now works as a fundraiser in Canada, told The Associated Press in a phone interview.

item.title: Coroner moved to tears by death of a child denied insulin on religious grounds
item.description:
Coroner moved to tears by death of a child denied insulin on religious grounds
An Australian coroner was moved to tears after hearing from the sister of an 8-year-old girl who died when her insulin was withheld by her parents on religious groundsByThe Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 6:23 AM
Share
BRISBANE, Australia -- An Australian coroner was moved to tears Thursday after hearing evidence from the older sister of an 8-year-old girl who died after her insulin was withheld by her parents on religious grounds.
Elizabeth Struhs died of ketoacidosis poisoning in 2022 after her father, Jason Struhs, denied her insulin for her type-1 diabetes.
Elizabeth’s parents, brother and another 11 members of a religious group that rejects modern medicine were convicted last year of Elizabeth’s manslaughter. The 14 members of the congregation, which called itself the "Saints," had gathered around her to pray as she lay dying.
Elizabeth's sister, Jayde Struhs, gave an emotional statement Thursday on the final day of an eight-day coroner's court inquiry in Brisbane into the death. Jayde had fled the family in 2014 at the age of 16, having rejected their religious views. She spoke of a sister who was never allowed experiences that ordinary people enjoy.
“Having Elizabeth in our lives is something we would have loved,” Jayde said. “She would have had everyone helping her manage her diabetes, her health and her learning. She would have learned about Christmas and the joy of being spoiled rotten.”
Through tears, Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard thanked Jayde for her recollections.

item.title: Venezuela claims to have 300Bn barrels of oil in the ground. Experts claim maybe
item.description:
Venezuela claims to have 300Bn barrels of oil in the ground. Experts claim maybe
One figure sets Venezuela apart from the rest of the world: 303 billion barrels of so-called proven oil reservesByREGINA GARCIA CANO Associated Press and COLLIN BINKLEY Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 6:06 AM
A single figure sets Venezuela apart from the rest of the world: 303 billion barrels of so-called proven oil reserves. But experts say the country's estimate is inherently problematic and far from proven — rooted in exaggerated, aging data from a corrupt government.
The number has long been touted by politicians and investors as an important measure of untapped energy potential, most recently by President Donald Trump's administration in detailing a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan reserves.
But a more realistic estimate of the country’s proven reserves — a gold standard metric, representing the amount of oil that can reasonably be extracted under current conditions — is about one-third of what it has reported, half a dozen experts told The Associated Press. They put the likely figure at 60 to 120 billion barrels, a vast amount but not enough for Venezuela to remain the world’s largest holder of reserves.
The distinction is an important one as Venezuela and the U.S. attempt to attract new investment into the country’s dilapidated oil industry, and it suggests that the deal Trump announced in August claiming the U.S. would ultimately control more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves is much less profitable than he asserted.
“That’s a funny, funny proposal,” Evanan Romero, a former Venezuela energy official now based in Houston, said of the deal, adding that he believes the Trump administration didn't fully research the South American country’s claims before wading in. “If the U.S. government called them and asked them to testify to how they did the procedure — well, the whole world will know that that’s a fun...

item.title: European Union awards top rights prize to International Criminal Court days after Trump sanctions
item.description:
European Union awards top rights prize to International Criminal Court days after Trump sanctions
The International Criminal Court and its embattled staff have won the European Union’s top human rights honorByLORNE COOK Associated Press and MIKE CORDER Associated PressOctober 22, 2026, 6:05 AM
Share
BRUSSELS -- The International Criminal Court and its embattled staff have won the European Union’s top human rights honor, the Sakharov Prize, an official said Thursday.
The award came just days after the Trump administration announced sweeping new sanctions on the court, which is based in The Hague, Netherlands, as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said.
Her announcement at the parliament in Strasbourg, France, was greeted with a standing ovation.
The annual EU award, named after Soviet dissident and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Andrei Sakharov, was created in 1988 to honor individuals or groups who defend human rights and basic freedoms.
ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan welcomed the award, saying that it “comes at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” she said in a statement.
The ICC opened in 2002 as a court of last resort to prosecute senior leaders it deems responsible for crimes that, according to its founding treaty, “deeply shock the conscience of humanity.” It has jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
